lessons.title: SELECT and Projection
lessons.concept: SQL retrieves data from tables. SELECT specifies which columns (projection) to return. FROM specifies the source table. Use specific columns instead of SELECT * when you know what you need for clarity and efficiency.
lessons.formula: SELECT column1, column2 FROM table_name; SELECT * FROM table_name; SELECT DISTINCT column1 FROM table_name;
lessons.worked_example: Given employees(id, name, department, salary): SELECT name, salary FROM employees; returns only those two columns for every row. SELECT DISTINCT department FROM employees; returns each department value once.
mistakes: Using SELECT * in production queries when only a few columns are needed.
Assuming SELECT without ORDER BY guarantees row order (it does not).
Forgetting that DISTINCT applies to the selected row/column combination, not just one column in isolation when multiple columns are selected.

lessons.title: Filtering Rows with WHERE
lessons.concept: WHERE filters rows before grouping/aggregation (except in some dialect-specific cases) by applying conditions. Conditions can use comparison operators (=, <>, <, >, <=, >=), logical operators (AND, OR, NOT), and predicates like IN, BETWEEN, LIKE, IS NULL.
lessons.formula: SELECT ... FROM table_name WHERE condition; Examples: WHERE salary > 50000 AND department = 'IT'; WHERE name LIKE 'A%'; WHERE manager_id IS NULL;
lessons.worked_example: SELECT name FROM employees WHERE department = 'Sales' AND salary >= 40000; returns names of Sales employees earning at least 40000. LIKE 'A%' matches strings starting with A; '%' matches any sequence, '_' matches a single character.
mistakes: Using = NULL instead of IS NULL (NULL comparisons require IS NULL / IS NOT NULL).
Confusing AND/OR precedence; use parentheses for clarity: WHERE (dept='IT' OR dept='HR') AND active=1.
Using LIKE without understanding wildcards or case-sensitivity behavior of the database.

lessons.title: Sorting and Limiting Results
lessons.concept: ORDER BY sorts result rows by one or more columns in ascending (ASC, default) or descending (DESC) order. LIMIT/TOP/FETCH restricts the number of rows returned (syntax varies by database). Sorting is often applied after filtering.
lessons.formula: SELECT ... FROM table_name WHERE ... ORDER BY column1 ASC, column2 DESC LIMIT n; (MySQL/PostgreSQL style; SQL Server uses TOP, standard SQL uses FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY.)
lessons.worked_example: SELECT name, salary FROM employees WHERE department = 'IT' ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 3; returns the top 3 highest-paid IT employees by salary. Multi-column sort: ORDER BY department ASC, salary DESC sorts by department first, then salary within each department.
mistakes: Assuming LIMIT without ORDER BY gives 'top' rows meaningfully (result set order is not guaranteed).
Confusing ASC/DESC on the wrong column in multi-column sorts.
Forgetting dialect differences (LIMIT vs TOP vs FETCH) in interviews; explain the concept clearly.

lessons.title: Aliases and Expressions
lessons.concept: Column aliases rename output columns for readability using AS (often optional). Expressions compute derived values in SELECT, such as salary*12 as annual_salary. Aliases defined in SELECT may not be usable in WHERE in many SQL engines (use the expression or a subquery/CTE depending on context).
lessons.formula: SELECT column AS alias FROM table; SELECT salary * 12 AS annual_salary FROM employees; SELECT first_name || ' ' || last_name AS full_name ... (concatenation syntax varies).
lessons.worked_example: SELECT name, salary, salary * 0.10 AS bonus FROM employees; computes bonus per row. Aliases improve reports and intermediate reasoning, but filtering on computed values may require repeating the expression in WHERE or using a derived table.
mistakes: Expecting SELECT aliases to work in WHERE in all databases.
Using ambiguous column names in joins without table aliases/prefixes.
Ignoring NULL behavior in expressions (e.g., arithmetic with NULL yields NULL in standard SQL).

practice.question: Which query returns only unique department values from an employees table?
practice.explanation: DISTINCT removes duplicate values from the result set for the selected columns. SELECT department returns all rows including duplicates. UNIQUE is a constraint concept in some contexts, but the standard query keyword for unique result rows is DISTINCT.

practice.question: Which condition correctly finds rows where manager_id has no value (NULL)?
practice.explanation: NULL represents unknown/missing value and cannot be compared with = in standard SQL. IS NULL checks for NULL values; IS NOT NULL checks for non-NULL values.

practice.question: What does this query return? SELECT name FROM employees WHERE salary > 50000 ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 5;

options.C: All employees with salary above 50000 in random order
options.D: First 5 employees inserted with salary above 50000

practice.explanation: WHERE filters employees with salary > 50000. ORDER BY salary DESC sorts them from highest to lowest salary. LIMIT 5 returns the first 5 rows of that sorted result, i.e., the 5 highest-paid among those matching the filter.
practice.provenance: Authored original practice item; not scraped.

practice.question: In a LIKE pattern, what does '%' represent?
practice.explanation: In SQL LIKE patterns, '%' matches any sequence of zero or more characters, and '_' matches exactly one character. For example, 'A%' matches 'A', 'An', 'Alice'.

practice.question: Which query correctly selects employees in either IT or HR departments with salary at least 30000?

options.A: SELECT * FROM employees WHERE department = 'IT' OR department = 'HR' AND salary >= 30000;
options.B: SELECT * FROM employees WHERE (department = 'IT' OR department = 'HR') AND salary >= 30000;
options.C: SELECT * FROM employees WHERE department = 'IT' AND 'HR' AND salary >= 30000;
options.D: SELECT * FROM employees WHERE department IN 'IT','HR' AND salary >= 30000;

practice.explanation: AND has higher precedence than OR in SQL, so option A would be interpreted as department='IT' OR (department='HR' AND salary>=30000), which can include IT employees below 30000. Parentheses in option B make the intent explicit and correct. A clearer alternative is WHERE department IN ('IT','HR') AND salary >= 30000.

questions.question: Given table students(id, name, marks), which query returns names of students scoring between 60 and 80 inclusive?

options.A: SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks > 60 AND marks < 80;
options.B: SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks BETWEEN 60 AND 80;
options.C: SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks IN (60, 80);
options.D: SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks = 60 OR 80;

questions.explanation: BETWEEN 60 AND 80 is inclusive of both endpoints in standard SQL. Option A excludes 60 and 80. Option C matches only exactly 60 or 80. Option D is invalid logic/syntax for this intent.

questions.question: What is the result of SELECT 5 + NULL; in standard SQL behavior?
questions.explanation: In standard SQL, arithmetic or comparison with NULL generally yields NULL because NULL means unknown. Some environments may display it differently, but the logical result is NULL.

questions.question: Which query lists products sorted by category ascending and, within each category, by price descending?

options.A: SELECT * FROM products ORDER BY category, price;
options.B: SELECT * FROM products ORDER BY category ASC, price DESC;
options.C: SELECT * FROM products ORDER BY price DESC, category ASC;
options.D: SELECT * FROM products ORDER BY DESC category, ASC price;

questions.explanation: ORDER BY supports multiple keys in priority order. category ASC sorts categories alphabetically/ascending first; for rows with same category, price DESC sorts higher prices first. Option A defaults price to ASC. Option D has invalid syntax.

questions.question: Which statement about SELECT * is most accurate?

options.A: It is always faster than selecting specific columns
options.B: It returns all columns from the referenced table(s)
options.D: It sorts rows by primary key

questions.explanation: SELECT * projects all columns available from the source in the query context. It does not remove duplicates (DISTINCT does) and does not guarantee order (ORDER BY does). It can be less efficient than selecting needed columns, especially with wide tables or joins.

questions.question: Table orders has columns (id, customer_id, amount, status). Which query returns customer_id and amount for delivered orders with amount over 1000?

options.A: SELECT customer_id, amount FROM orders WHERE status = 'delivered' OR amount > 1000;
options.B: SELECT customer_id, amount FROM orders WHERE status = 'delivered' AND amount > 1000;
options.C: SELECT customer_id AND amount FROM orders WHERE status = 'delivered', amount > 1000;
options.D: SELECT (customer_id, amount) WHERE orders.status = delivered AND amount > 1000;

questions.explanation: We need both conditions true: status is delivered and amount exceeds 1000, so use AND. Option A uses OR and would include non-delivered orders above 1000 or delivered orders at/below 1000. Options C and D are not valid SQL syntax for this query.
